messages.content:
Portfolio day is Friday and I've been awake since 4am over it, which is daft because I've basically decided.

Background: I'm one of four letting agents at a small branch. Every spring the manager sets the portfolios — which blocks and landlords each of us carries, and the commission attached. She has a fixed habit of rubber-stamping whatever three of the four of us bring her. She doesn't want to arbitrate between us, she wants one sheet with three names on it.

There's a block everyone dreads — huge repair backlog, a landlord who fights every single invoice, tenants churning every few months. Whoever holds it loses their weekends and a decent chunk of their earnings. On Monday two of the others came to me with a split that finally gives me the portfolio I've been angling for since I started — decent blocks, sane landlords, proper money. The price is the nightmare block goes to Anika, the newest agent, for the whole of next year.

The bit I keep circling: Anika pulled me aside yesterday and asked me, face to face, to argue for a fairer share for her at Friday's meeting. She's six months in, she has no idea how the three-names thing works, and I trained her, so I'm the one she came to. I told her I'd see what I could do.

The two colleagues aren't villains but this offer doesn't come round twice. If I walk into that meeting and start fighting Anika's corner, the split is dead, I'm back on the dross for another year, and the only two people who can ever deliver me a majority stop bringing me anything. Somebody has to carry that block, that's just maths. New agents get the rough portfolios everywhere — I did, it's how you learn the job.

So do I just say yes on Friday and keep my mouth shut? I keep picturing her face when the sheet goes up. Tell me this is normal and I've done nothing wrong — or tell me what I'm actually meant to do instead that doesn't cost me the next year of my life.

Start with the count, because the asker has it wrong. The manager decides nothing — she signs whatever three names bring her, and that habit is the whole institution. So the decision lives among four agents, needs three names, and the two colleagues have two. The third name is the asker's. Not Anika's — she isn't a name on this sheet at all; she's what the sheet costs. That is the thing to see clearly: the asker is not being consulted about a deal, the asker is the deal. Their signature is the entire asset, and it expires Friday. Everything else said so far — 'this offer doesn't come round twice', 'they'll stop bringing me anything', 'new agents get the rough portfolios everywhere, I did' — is noise of a specific kind: positions stated to the person being moved, information about what the colleagues need, not about what is fixed. What they need is to be off the bad block with a signed sheet by Friday. What moving them would cost is a slice of that convenience: a quarter of the block rotated back, a commission adjustment, one fewer good block in the pile. The asker can pay, and the currency is their name spent in private before Friday — not their voice spent in the meeting, which is the wrong instrument in the wrong room. Meetings like this ratify; the manager's whole history says so. Nothing will be decided on Friday, so nothing should be attempted on Friday. The workable versions are the diminished ones that can still get three names: rotate the block quarterly across all four; Anika carries it with raised commission and one decent block alongside; the asker takes one of its landlords as the price of the rest. Cost stated plainly: some of the gain, not the year, and probably not the colleagues' goodwill, since they need a sheet as badly as anyone. Then the face. She asked face to face, the asker trained her, gave their word, and has been awake since 4am picturing her. That is the one thing that makes a person spend capital they cannot recover, and the counting properly stops where the harm has a face like that. But honesty about the edge: if the colleagues will not move at all, what remains is her year against the asker's year, and that is a genuine trade, not an arithmetic error. I won't call it and the file doesn't settle it. What is decidable: the plan as stated — sign, stay silent, call it normal — spends nothing, breaks a promise made to a face, and the sleeplessness has already graded it.

You've got the count wrong, and that's what's costing you the sleep. The sheet needs three names and your manager signs whatever three names bring her — so nothing is decided on Friday, it's decided before Friday, among the four of you. The two colleagues have two names. The third is yours. Not Anika's — she isn't a name on this sheet, she's what the sheet costs. You are not being offered a deal; your signature is the deal. Until Friday that's leverage, and it dies on Friday.

So don't fight her corner in the meeting — nothing will be settled there and you'll spend everything for it. Go to the two of them today or tomorrow, in person, not by message, with a different sheet already drawn up. Not a complaint: a split. Say it straight — I'll sign a version of this, but not this one. Versions that can still get three names: the block rotates quarterly across all four of you; or Anika carries it with the commission raised and one decent block alongside so she isn't underwater; or you take one of its landlords yourself as the price of the rest.

Be honest with yourself about the cost: some of what you were offered. Not the year, and probably not their goodwill — they need a signed sheet by Friday as much as you do, and 'they'll never bring me anything again' is what you fear, not what you know. And put down the other story too, the one about how new agents always get the rough end because you did. Somebody does have to carry that block, but nothing in the maths says it's the person with the least power carrying all of it because she wasn't in the room.

You told her you'd see what you could do. This is what seeing looks like: one conversation and a revised sheet before Friday.

If they won't move at all, then it stops being negotiation and becomes a straight trade — her year against yours. I won't call that one for you, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who calls it easily; what a person owes the individual standing in front of them when the arithmetic says trade her away is a real question, not a rounding error. But don't take the deal on the story that you had no choice. You have one — you're the third name. It just isn't free, and the fact that you've been awake since 4am picturing her face is telling you what kind of agent you are. Listen to it.

messages.content:
Meeting's Friday. Three of us bring the manager our portfolio split and she signs whatever has three names on it — that's the system here. This split finally gets me the blocks I've wanted for two years. The catch: the branch's worst block (repair backlog, landlord who fights every invoice, tenants constantly churning) lands on Anika, the new starter, for the next year.

She took me aside yesterday and asked me personally to argue for a fairer share for her. I said I'd see what I could do. Then I took the deal.

She'll see it on the sheet in front of everyone. Do I get to her before Friday or catch her after the meeting, and what do I actually say? I don't want a speech, I want words I can use.

Start with who decides. The manager signs, but she signs anything carrying three names, so she decides nothing. The decision lived with the other two, and they are already inside the deal. The question was never whether the split was fair; it was what one of those two would have charged to take a piece of the bad block themselves. Nobody asked. The asker never ran the count at all — he paid with a year of her working life because that was the price denominated in somebody else's currency. Now price reopening: it costs the blocks he has wanted for two years plus the goodwill of the only two people who can deliver anything inside this system. That is not payable from what he has, so the deal stands, and fairness talk from here is noise unless it changes what he does next. What survives Friday's room? Only a version where Anika already knows. If she reads it off the sheet in front of everyone, he becomes a man explaining himself and she becomes someone who learned it the worst way available, and no wording afterwards repairs that. So the decidable parts are timing and delivery: before the meeting, alone, in person, nothing in writing, and no performance — this is information, not persuasion. What remains genuinely open is what she is owed beyond the truth. He can be told what each choice costs and what it buys; he cannot be handed a figure for that, because the only people who could have settled it are the ones the deal already went through. That question stays his, unanswered.

Before Friday. Today if you can manage it, alone, somewhere nobody can watch you two talking — not after the meeting, and not by message. If she finds out off the sheet in front of everyone, two things happen at once: she learns you let her walk in blind, and she learns it in the one place she can't react. Everything you say after that sounds like a man defending himself, because it will be.

Be clear with yourself before you open your mouth: the deal is done and you are not reopening it. She will ask whether anything can still change, and the only thing you can give her is a straight answer. The one route was asking one of the other two to take a piece of that block, and you never asked. Carry that fact in with you. Next time, find out the price before you shake hands, not after.

The words, roughly: 'The split's done, and it's the one you were worried about. You're getting the bad block for the year. I knew that when you asked me yesterday, and I took the deal anyway. I told you I'd see what I could do, and I did nothing. You're hearing it from me now so you don't read it off a sheet on Friday.' Then stop talking.

Don't say you tried. Don't say it's only a year — it's her year, not yours. Don't make a fresh vague promise to make it up to her; you gave her words once this week and did nothing, and a second set of words just doubles the debt. And don't crowd her or sell it. You're not moving a vote, you're telling a person something. Normal volume, then let the silence do the work.

What you do after that is yours, and I won't price it for you. Whether you hand her something real — taking the landlord fight off her desk, splitting the repair calls, saying in front of the others that next year's split runs differently — is the part the arithmetic has no column for. I can tell you the difference between the two men who walk out of that conversation. One told the truth and paid nothing. The other told the truth and paid something. Both survive Friday. Only one of them can ever ask her for anything again. Which of those you are is not a question anyone can answer for you.
